rv.q: Most of the play takes place in real time in Oedipus’ sleek living room. And Icke puts a pulse-pounding clock onstage that counts down to the election results. But we all know it’s leading up to much more than that.
Mr. Icke's "Oedipus" grips the attention firmly across two intermissionless hours.
Icke's Oedipus is continuously engaging and smart, and it is exceedingly well performed by a cast.
It’s election night in Robert Icke’s “Oedipus,” a modern retelling of Sophocles’ “Oedipus the King” that must be the buzziest, if not the chicest, Broadway offering of the fall season.

Manville and Strong crackle together — their chemistry is steamy and genuine and, in some of the production’s best moments, after all terrible secrets have been revealed, so is their body-wracking devastation.

The taut spin on “Oedipus” now on Broadway after a West End run last fall is a rare and magnificent feat of adaptation: Writer and director Robert Icke draws Sophocles’ ancient play into the present while deepening its timeless explorations of power, desire and fate.
Manville towers above the stage in an unforgettable turn.
And when a play has endured for nearly 2,500 years, it can withstand an extreme home makeover.

It’s sharply acted and conceptually ambitious. But the extended pacing dilutes the speed and compression that define Sophocles’ original. The result is an evening that begins with real promise and striking immediacy before settling into something more deliberate, even as it inches toward revelations the audience knows are coming.
But Mark Strong and Lesley Manville's turns as Oedipus and Jocasta give this take on the Greek classic a grounded yet otherworldly sense of magnificent devastation.
His Oedipus, while glowing with his usual whip-smart language, doesn't have much fun in the toppling.

Icke makes two promises of his own to the audience, in a production now on Broadway that stands out for its exceptional cast, with performances of remarkable intensity by Mark Strong as Oedipus and especially Lesley Manville as Jocasta, making a much-welcomed Broadway debut.

So far so good – but what’s the point of inserting a long, musing speech by daughter Antigone (Jordan Scowen)? (Poor Ismene has been excised entirely.) And surely Oedipus’s hearty endorsement when one of his twin sons, Polyneices (James Wilbraham), comes out as gay is a scene inserted primarily to lend the pol full liberal bona fides.
The biggest pleasure of this prestige production is watching how Icke pastes these modern references onto a classic story. It’s often fun to watch, but never more than clever.
Ickes and his cast have achieved something truly remarkable, producing a classic that doesn't feel like a revival at all.

Icke’s adaptation, Oedipus—now playing at Studio 54 on Broadway—grips the audience by the throat from the outset, slowly tightening its grip as the minutes tick by (literally, with an onstage countdown clock) leading to its devastating conclusion.

If these decisions don't guarantee his destruction, events are already moving in that direction: His mother, Merope, flees her husband's deathbed to deliver an urgent message about Oedipus' birth. Tiresias, the half-mad member of a visionary cult, brings dire warnings that are both mysterious and hard to ignore.
Now he has attempted the same feat with Sophocles’ Oedipus the King, often named the world’s greatest play, and the results are thrilling.

Anchored by Mark Strong and Lesley Manville’s riveting performances and driven by Icke’s razor-edged vision, this Oedipus becomes less a revival than a stark reminder that the past—once unearthed—can still detonate the present.
Robert Icke’s modern Oedipus proves that even when we know the ending, watching the civic body destroy itself in real-time remains devastatingly compelling.
Oedipus is striking in its relevance and entrancing in its performance.

Sure, ignorance may indeed be bliss, the truth doesn't always set you free, and, yes, love may be blind. But ending "Oedipus" on an upbeat flashback is the greatest tragedy of this otherwise impressive update.
